finding: The risk of delay climbs through the day
number: 13% of flights scheduled between 6 and 9 am are late or cancelled, against 40% between 7 and 10 pm (3.0 times as often).
check_result: Resampling whole days (flights on one day are not independent): evening is 3.0 times the morning rate (95% interval 2.7 to 3.2); morning 13.4% (12.3%-14.6%), evening 39.6% (36.9%-42.4%). A flight-level chi-square gives p < 0.001 but is optimistic.
action: Offer morning flights to clients with a tight connection or an important meeting, and put evening flights first in the list to warn.
why: Not crowding: airports handle about 23 departures per hour in the morning and 19 in the evening. Delays seem to pile up as the day goes on; finding 2 looks at one way this can happen.

finding: When a plane's earlier flight ran late, its next flight is much more likely to be late (the domino effect)
number: When the same plane's earlier flight left more than 15 minutes late, 61% of the next flights are late or cancelled, against 25% when it left on time.
check_result: Resampling whole days: the gap is 37 points (95% interval 35 to 38); 13,513 flights after a late flight, 82,490 after an on-time one. Within the same day, airport and part of the day the gap is 26 points against 37 overall.
action: Two hours before departure, look at the same plane's earlier flights today. If one ran late, warn the client early and prepare a backup.
why: A delay can travel forward because planes, crews and gates are shared, but part of the gap is a bad day hitting both flights: within the same day, airport and part of the day the gap is 26 points instead of 37. It shows in the morning, afternoon and evening alike (see the chart), so it is not just the time-of-day effect. We can show the link, not prove the cause.

finding: Airlines differ a lot in reliability
number: Among the 9 biggest airlines, Republic Airline has 18% of flights late or cancelled and JetBlue Airways has 35%.
check_result: Resampling whole days: the worst airline's rate is 2.0 times the best airline's (95% interval 1.8 to 2.2); Republic Airline 17.6%, JetBlue Airways 35.1%. The best and the worst were picked from the same data, so the size of the gap is somewhat flattering; the gap is wide enough for the order to hold.
action: When a client has a tight connection, prefer the more reliable airlines; warn clients on the least reliable ones earlier.
why: Compared only with flights from the same airport in the same part of the day, JetBlue Airways runs at 1.36 times the expected rate and Republic Airline at 0.67 (1.00 = as expected). A ratio far from 1.00 means airport and time of day do not explain the gap.

finding: A late earlier flight goes with a bigger jump in risk than everyday bad weather does
number: In bad weather 36% of flights are late or cancelled, against 24% in calm weather. Among flights whose plane had already flown earlier that day, a late earlier flight adds 36 points and bad weather adds 18.
check_result: Resampling whole days: the late earlier flight's jump is 18 points bigger than the bad-weather jump (the difference between the two jumps, 95% interval 13 to 22); on its own, bad weather adds 12 points to the rate over all flights (95% interval 9 to 15; 55,646 flights in bad weather, 275,237 in calm weather).
action: Use the weather report as a trigger to warn clients ahead of a stormy day, and the earlier-flight check as the stronger signal for individual flights.
why: Bad weather cuts the number of flights an airport can handle, so queues form. A late earlier flight goes with a bigger jump in risk in these data, although part of that jump is a shared bad day (finding 2). We can compare the two jumps, but not say what causes each. The comparison is with everyday bad weather as defined above (flights with a missing gust reading count as calm). With stricter definitions the weather jump gets larger but covers very few flights (visibility under 1 mile: +29 points, 149 flights; gusts of 35 mph or more: +23 points, 163 flights; rain or snow of 0.1 inch or more: +64 points, 80 flights), against 36 points for a late earlier flight.

finding: Cancellations come in waves on a few days, mostly in summer
number: The 10 worst days hold 35% of all cancellations from January to September. July had 8.7% of flights cancelled against 1.5% in January and February.
check_result: Across 273 days, the daily cancellation rate and the heaviest hourly rain at the airports rise together only moderately: rank correlation 0.39, p < 0.001.
action: Do not wait for winter: watch for summer storm days. Keep backup options for clients ready, and rebook early when airlines or air-traffic alerts announce disruption, since New York weather alone does not predict these days.
why: Odd at first, since snow is the usual suspect. The weather at our three airports explains only part of it: daily cancellations rise with rain (rank correlation 0.39), but 4 of the 5 worst days had rain at the time of fewer than 3 in 10 flights and 5 had no gusts of 25 mph at all. Storms elsewhere on the routes or air-traffic limits are not in our data, so that remains a guess. The data cannot tell us why winter 2023 was calmer.
